entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A question that is hard to answer, because the honest answer is complicated, unclear or awkward to give.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, interviews and teaching; *tricky* is more informal than *difficult* and suggests the question needs care or has a hidden catch. People often say *That's a tricky question* to buy a few seconds before answering. In formal writing, *a difficult question* or *a challenging question* is more usual.
entries.pattern: ask (someone) a tricky question; that's a tricky question
examples: My five-year-old asked me where babies come from, which is **a tricky question** to answer over breakfast.
The interviewer asked me **a tricky question** about why I'd left my last job after only six months.
Whether you should tip at a self-checkout kiosk is **a tricky question** these days.

drill.sentence: When the reporter asked if he'd play another season, the quarterback smiled and said, "That's {{a tricky question}}."
drill.hint: one that's hard to answer well (the adjective is not *tough*, *hard*, *difficult* or *good*)

entries.related: *a tough question* — similar, stresses difficulty rather than a catch; *a trick question* — a question designed to make you answer wrongly; *a loaded question* — one that contains an unfair assumption.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To accept and deal with the bad results that your own actions or decisions cause.
entries.usage: Common in parenting, news and work, often as a warning: *If you break the rules, you'll have to face the consequences.* Typical frames are *have to face the consequences*, *face the consequences of* + noun or *-ing*, and *face serious / legal consequences*. *Suffer the consequences* is similar but stresses the pain more.
entries.pattern: face the consequences (of + noun / -ing)
examples: You lied to your teacher, so now you'll have to **face the consequences**.
Companies that dump waste into the river should **face the consequences** of their actions.
I stayed up until three binge-watching a show, and today I'm **facing the consequences**.

drill.sentence: Parents who always rescue their kids from trouble never let them {{face the consequences}} of their own choices.
drill.hint: experience the results personally (the verb is not *suffer*, *accept*, *live with* or *deal with*)

mistake.wrong: If you cheat on the test, you'll have to carry the consequences.
mistake.right: If you cheat on the test, you'll have to face the consequences.
mistake.why: German *die Konsequenzen tragen* is *face* or *bear the consequences* in English; *carry* sounds wrong here.

entries.related: *suffer the consequences* — stresses the pain; *bear the consequences* — more formal; *get away with it* — the opposite, avoid any punishment.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: For now; for a period that will probably end when the situation changes.
entries.usage: Common in speech, emails and public notices; it signals that an arrangement is temporary but has no fixed end date. It usually comes at the start or the end of the clause. It sounds slightly more formal and more clearly temporary than *for now*.
entries.pattern: For the time being, …; … for the time being
examples: Our new apartment isn't ready, so we're living with my parents **for the time being**.
The public pool will stay closed **for the time being** while the city repairs the roof.
**For the time being**, I'm happy working part-time and spending more time with the baby.

drill.sentence: The bakery has stopped making its famous croissants {{for the time being}}, but the owner says they'll be back by spring.
drill.hint: until things change (not *for now*, *for the moment* or *for a while*)

entries.related: *for now* — shorter, more casual; *for the moment* — very similar; *until further notice* — formal, used in official notices.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To support one person or group against another in an argument or conflict.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about family, friends and arguments at work, very often in the negative: *I'm not taking sides* or *I don't want to take sides*. The plural *sides* is the usual form; to name the person you support, say *take someone's side* or *side with* someone. It often suggests that staying neutral would be wiser.
entries.pattern: take sides (in + argument); take someone's side
examples: When my parents argue, I try not to **take sides**, because I love them both.
The referee is supposed to be neutral, but fans of both teams accused him of **taking sides**.
Most of the office **took sides** in the fight between the two managers, and the atmosphere got tense.

drill.sentence: My two best friends aren't speaking to each other, and I refuse to {{take sides}}.
drill.hint: support one of them against the other (the verb is not *pick* or *choose*)

mistake.wrong: I don't want to take party in their argument.
mistake.right: I don't want to take sides in their argument.
mistake.why: German *Partei ergreifen* is *take sides* in English; *party* means a political party or a celebration.

entries.related: *side with someone* — support a named person; *pick sides* — very similar, informal; *stay out of it* — the opposite, remain neutral.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A good chance to do or get something that was not used, and that may not come again.
entries.usage: Common in sports commentary, business, journalism and conversation about the past; it usually sounds regretful or critical. Typical frames are *It was a missed opportunity (to* + verb*)* and *a big / huge missed opportunity*. The verb form is *miss an opportunity*: *Don't miss this opportunity.*
entries.pattern: a (huge) missed opportunity (to + verb / for + someone)
examples: Not asking her out before she moved to Atlanta was **a missed opportunity** I still think about.
The team had three chances to score in the final minute. What **a missed opportunity**!
Many residents called the new train station **a missed opportunity** to add more bike parking.

drill.sentence: The company could have bought the startup for almost nothing ten years ago, and the CEO now calls it {{a missed opportunity}}.
drill.hint: a good chance that slipped away (the adjective is not *lost* or *wasted*)

entries.related: *a lost opportunity* — very similar; *a wasted opportunity* — stronger, suggests carelessness; *seize an opportunity* — the opposite, use it fully.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Definitely worth the money, time or effort that something costs, so it is a good idea to do or buy it.
entries.usage: Very common in reviews, travel tips and recommendations: *The museum is well worth a visit.* Patterns are *well worth* + noun (*the money, the wait, the effort, a visit*), *well worth it* and *well worth* + *-ing*. *Very worth* is not idiomatic; use *well worth* or *really worth*.
entries.pattern: well worth + the wait / a visit / it / -ing
examples: The line was long, but the barbecue was **well worth the wait**.
If you're ever in Chicago, the architecture boat tour is **well worth it**.
Learning to cook a few basic meals is **well worth the effort** if you want to save money.

drill.sentence: The hike to the top is steep and takes three hours, but the view is {{well worth}} it.
drill.hint: more than repays the effort (the adverb is not *totally*, *really* or *definitely*)

mistake.wrong: This book is very worth reading.
mistake.right: This book is well worth reading.
mistake.why: *Worth* is not a normal adjective, so *very* cannot go before it; English uses *well worth* or *really worth*.

entries.related: *worth it* — informal, without the intensifier; *worthwhile* — adjective before a noun: *a worthwhile trip*; *not worth the trouble* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To do things in advance to prevent danger, damage or other problems.
entries.usage: Common in safety advice, health information, news and workplace instructions. Patterns are *take precautions against* + risk and *take (extra / necessary / basic) precautions to* + verb; the noun is almost always plural. In casual speech people often just say *be careful* or *play it safe*.
entries.pattern: take (extra / the necessary) precautions against + noun / to + verb
examples: Hikers should **take precautions** against ticks, like wearing long pants and checking their skin afterward.
We **took extra precautions** when the baby started crawling and covered every outlet in the house.
Before the hurricane hit, the city **took precautions** to protect the hospital's power supply.

drill.sentence: Before you leave on vacation, {{take precautions}} so burglars can't tell nobody's home, like putting your lights on a timer.
drill.hint: do sensible things in advance to stay safe (the noun is not *steps* or *measures*)

mistake.wrong: We made some precautions before the storm.
mistake.right: We took some precautions before the storm.
mistake.why: *Precautions* goes with *take*; German *Vorkehrungen treffen* tempts learners to use *make*.

entries.related: *take steps* — act to deal with something; *play it safe* — informal, avoid risk; *throw caution to the wind* — the opposite.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: When you first look at something, before you examine it closely; the first impression often turns out to be wrong.
entries.usage: Common in writing, journalism and explanations, usually at the start of a sentence and followed by a contrast (*At first glance it looks simple, but …*). There is no article, and the preposition is *at*. *At first sight* is similar but is best known from *love at first sight*.
entries.pattern: At first glance, … (but …)
examples: **At first glance**, the apartment seemed perfect, but then we noticed the water stains on the ceiling.
The two paintings look identical **at first glance**, yet one of them is a cheap copy.
Even **at first glance**, it was clear the old car needed a lot of work.

drill.sentence: {{At first glance}}, the puzzle looks easy, but most people need over an hour to finish it.
drill.hint: before you look closely (the noun is not *sight*)

mistake.wrong: On the first glance, the plan looked fine.
mistake.right: At first glance, the plan looked fine.
mistake.why: German *auf den ersten Blick* becomes *at first glance*: the preposition is *at*, and there is no *the*.

entries.related: *at first sight* — similar, best known from *love at first sight*; *on the surface* — judging by appearances; *on closer inspection* — the opposite, after looking carefully.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To decide not to apply the usual rule in one particular case.
entries.usage: Common at work, in customer service, schools and family life, often in a polite request: *Could you make an exception just this once?* Patterns are *make an exception for* someone or something and *make an exception in this case*. The firm opposite is *make no exceptions*.
entries.pattern: make an exception (for + someone / in this case)
examples: I never eat dessert, but for my aunt's apple pie I'll **make an exception**.
The professor doesn't accept late work, but she **made an exception** because I'd been in the hospital.
Our landlord has a strict no-pets policy, but he **made an exception** for our old cat.

drill.sentence: The museum is closed on Mondays, but the director agreed to {{make an exception}} for a group of students who had driven all the way from Ohio.
drill.hint: not apply the usual rule just this once (not *bend the rules*)

entries.related: *bend the rules* — be flexible about rules, a little informal; *the exception to the rule* — a case that doesn't follow the general pattern; *no exceptions* — the rule applies to everyone.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: A reason to be worried about something.
entries.usage: Common in news, medicine, school reports and official statements; it sounds calm and measured. Typical frames are *be a (real / serious) cause for concern*, *There's no cause for concern* and *give cause for concern*. The article disappears after *no* and in *give cause for concern*.
entries.pattern: be a (serious) cause for concern; there's no cause for concern
examples: The doctor said that a little swelling after surgery is **no cause for concern**.
The growing number of empty storefronts downtown is **a real cause for concern**.
Her grades have slipped a bit this semester, but her teacher doesn't think it's **a cause for concern** yet.

drill.sentence: The leaves on my lemon tree are turning yellow, which could be {{a cause for concern}} if it keeps happening.
drill.hint: a reason to worry (the first noun is not *reason*; the second is not *alarm*)

entries.related: *cause for alarm* — stronger, a reason to be frightened; *a red flag* — informal, a warning sign; *nothing to worry about* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To find time for something or someone in a busy schedule, because you think it matters.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, advice and self-help writing; it suggests a deliberate choice: *You have to make time for exercise.* The patterns are *make time for* + noun and *make time to* + verb. Compare *have time for*, which only says that the time is available.
entries.pattern: make time for + noun / make time to + verb
examples: Even with two jobs, she **makes time for** a long walk every evening.
My dad was always busy, but he **made time** to come to every one of my games.
We both work late, so we have to **make time for** each other on weekends.

drill.sentence: No matter how busy you are, try to {{make time for}} the people who matter most to you.
drill.hint: fit them into your schedule on purpose (not *find* or *set aside*)

entries.related: *find time for* — similar, a little less deliberate; *set aside time for* — reserve time in advance; *not have time for* — the opposite, often a polite refusal.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Fully earned through effort, good work or good behavior, so that people agree it is fair.
entries.usage: Very common in congratulations, speeches, emails and sports reports. Before a noun it is usually hyphenated (*a well-deserved break*); after a verb it usually is not (*The win was well deserved*). Typical nouns are *break, rest, vacation, win, award* and *promotion*.
entries.pattern: a well-deserved + noun; be well deserved
examples: After working every weekend for two months, Sam finally took a **well-deserved** vacation.
Her award was **well deserved**; she's been running the food bank for twenty years.
Congratulations on the promotion, Maria. It's **well deserved**!

drill.sentence: The standing ovation at the end of her final concert was {{well deserved}}.
drill.hint: completely fair, given her talent and hard work (the participle is not *earned*)

entries.related: *well-earned* — very similar, often with *rest* or *break*; *hard-earned* — gained through hard work, often with *money*; *undeserved* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To be better or more successful than people expected.
entries.usage: Common in business, reviews, sports and performance evaluations, where it sounds slightly formal. Patterns are *exceed (all / my / everyone's) expectations* and *far exceed expectations*; *expectations* is plural. In conversation people often say *It was better than I expected*, and finance news often uses *beat expectations*.
entries.pattern: (far) exceed (all / someone's) expectations
examples: I thought the cheap motel would be awful, but it **exceeded my expectations**: the room was spotless.
The bake sale **far exceeded expectations** and raised over three thousand dollars for the school library.
Ticket sales for the small-town film festival **exceeded expectations**, so it's adding a second weekend.

drill.sentence: Honestly, my son's first loaf of homemade bread {{exceeded my expectations}}; it was actually delicious.
drill.hint: was better than I'd hoped (the verb is not *surpassed* or *beat*)

mistake.wrong: The trip overcame all my expectations.
mistake.right: The trip exceeded all my expectations.
mistake.why: *Overcome* means defeat a problem; for being better than expected, English uses *exceed*, *surpass* or *beat*.

entries.related: *surpass expectations* — same, a bit more formal; *live up to expectations* — be as good as expected; *fall short of expectations* — the opposite.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: By a large amount; used with superlatives to say that something is clearly the most, best or biggest.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, usually with a superlative: *by far the best* or *the best by far*. With a comparative, natives normally use *far* or *much* alone (*far better*). It never goes with a plain adjective.
entries.pattern: by far the + superlative; the + superlative + by far
examples: This is **by far** the best pizza I've had since moving to New York.
Rent is **by far** our biggest monthly expense.
Of all the people we interviewed, she was the most qualified **by far**.

drill.sentence: Driving is cheaper, but taking the train is {{by far}} the most relaxing way to get to the coast.
drill.hint: clearly, with a big gap to the rest (not *easily* or *definitely*)

mistake.wrong: The sequel is by far not as good as the original.
mistake.right: The sequel is nowhere near as good as the original.
mistake.why: German *bei weitem nicht* is *nowhere near* or *not nearly* in English; *by far* goes with superlatives.

entries.related: *easily* — informal, same use before superlatives: *easily the best*; *far* / *much* — with comparatives: *far better*; *nowhere near* — very far from it.

entries.label: noun + noun
entries.meaning: Signals that something bad, such as an illness, a crisis or a failure, may happen or is already starting.
entries.usage: Common in health advice, news, finance and talk about relationships. Patterns are *the warning signs of* + problem, *spot / recognize / ignore the warning signs* and *early warning signs*. It is usually plural; for one signal, say *a warning sign*.
entries.pattern: spot / ignore the (early) warning signs of + noun
examples: Chest pain and shortness of breath can be **warning signs** of a heart attack.
Looking back, there were plenty of **warning signs** that their marriage was in trouble.
Investors ignored the **warning signs**, and the company collapsed within a year.

drill.sentence: Parents should learn to recognize the {{warning signs}} of depression in teenagers, such as sudden changes in sleep or mood.
drill.hint: signals that something is wrong (not *red flags* or *symptoms*)

entries.related: *red flags* — informal, signs of a problem, especially in a person or a deal; *symptoms* — signs of an illness; *a wake-up call* — an event that makes you see a problem.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To officially give information or an opinion to the public, usually in writing, on behalf of a person or an organization.
entries.usage: Typical of news reports about companies, celebrities, hospitals, police and sports teams. Patterns are *issue a statement saying (that) …* and *in a statement issued on Monday*; *release a statement* is a common alternative. A person who speaks formally in public or to the police *makes a statement*.
entries.pattern: issue a statement (saying that … / about + noun)
examples: After the concert was canceled, the band **issued a statement** apologizing to fans.
The hospital **issued a statement** saying the patient was in stable condition.
On Friday, the school district **issued a statement** explaining why classes would start an hour late.

drill.sentence: Hours after the video went viral, the restaurant chain {{issued a statement}} promising to retrain its staff.
drill.hint: officially told the public in writing (the verb is not *released*, *made* or *put out*)

entries.related: *release a statement* — same; *make a statement* — say something formally, often in person; *decline to comment* — the opposite, refuse to say anything.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Able to cause harm in some situations or under some conditions, though not always or not yet.
entries.usage: Common in safety warnings, news, medicine and science writing; it sounds careful rather than alarming. It often comes before a noun (*a potentially dangerous situation*) and goes with *chemicals, side effects, conditions* and *animals*. *Potentially* also collocates with *fatal, harmful* and *life-threatening*.
entries.pattern: a potentially dangerous + noun; be potentially dangerous (to / for + someone)
examples: Mixing bleach with other cleaning products can produce **potentially dangerous** fumes.
Police described the escaped prisoner as **potentially dangerous** and told people not to approach him.
Leaving a toddler alone near a pool, even for a minute, is **potentially dangerous**.

drill.sentence: The weather service warned of {{potentially dangerous}} rip currents at the beach this weekend.
drill.hint: able to cause harm under some conditions (the adverb is not *possibly*; not *life-threatening*)

entries.related: *hazardous* — formal, dangerous, often of materials; *risky* — involving a chance of harm or loss; *harmless* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To start talking about something different, often to avoid an awkward or unpleasant topic.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and storytelling, and it often suggests avoidance: *Every time I ask about money, he changes the subject.* It can also be open and polite: *Can we change the subject?* The article *the* is fixed; *change the topic* is possible but much less common.
entries.pattern: (quickly / awkwardly) change the subject
examples: Every time I ask my brother about his new girlfriend, he quickly **changes the subject**.
Dinner was getting tense, so I **changed the subject** to everyone's summer plans.
When reporters asked about the rumors, the actor smiled and **changed the subject**.

drill.sentence: "So, how's the job search going?" "Can we please {{change the subject}}? I don't want to think about it tonight."
drill.hint: start talking about something else (not *switch topics* or *drop it*)

entries.related: *drop the subject* — stop talking about it; *steer the conversation* — guide it toward a topic; *beat around the bush* — avoid saying something directly.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Regularly; at times that are repeated, often at fixed intervals.
entries.usage: Common in emails, instructions, business and medical writing; it is longer and slightly more formal than *regularly*. It usually comes at the end of the clause, and the adjective can change: *on a daily / weekly / monthly basis*. In casual speech it can sound wordy, so *regularly* or *all the time* is often better.
entries.pattern: on a regular / daily / weekly basis
examples: Our upstairs neighbors throw loud parties **on a regular basis**, usually on Friday nights.
It's a good idea to back up the photos on your phone **on a regular basis**.
The restaurant is inspected by the health department **on a regular basis**.

drill.sentence: My doctor told me to check my blood pressure {{on a regular basis}}, not just when I feel sick.
drill.hint: at repeated times (a longer phrase than *regularly*; the adjective is not *daily*)

mistake.wrong: We see our cousins on regular basis.
mistake.right: We see our cousins on a regular basis.
mistake.why: The phrase needs the article *a*: *on a regular / daily / weekly basis*.

entries.related: *regularly* — shorter and more natural in speech; *on a daily basis* — every day; *from time to time* — only occasionally.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Messages or behavior that suggest opposite things, so it is hard to know what someone really thinks or wants.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation about dating and relationships, and also used about bosses, companies and markets. The usual patterns are *send / give (someone) mixed signals* and *get mixed signals from* someone. It is almost always plural; *mixed messages* means the same.
entries.pattern: send / give someone mixed signals; get mixed signals from someone
examples: He texts me every night but never wants to meet up. He's sending me **mixed signals**.
Kids get **mixed signals** when one parent says yes and the other says no.
Management is giving **mixed signals**: they want us back in the office, but they've just sold half the desks.

drill.sentence: First she invited me to her birthday, and then she ignored me all night. I'm getting {{mixed signals}}.
drill.hint: behavior that points in two directions (the noun is not *messages*)

entries.related: *mixed messages* — same; *blow hot and cold* — keep changing your attitude toward someone; *a clear signal* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To expect that something or someone will be very successful.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports, business and family talk, with a person or a thing after *for*. It often comes before a disappointment: *We had high hopes for the new coach, but …* The negative *I don't have high hopes* means you expect little.
entries.pattern: have high hopes for + someone / something
examples: We **had high hopes for** the new Italian place, but the pasta was overcooked and cold.
Her parents **have high hopes for** her, since she's the first in the family to go to college.
The coach **has high hopes for** this year's team, which has lost only one game so far.

drill.sentence: The rabbits ate half the garden, so I don't {{have high hopes for}} this year's tomatoes.
drill.hint: expect much from (the adjective is not *great* or *big*)

mistake.wrong: We have big hopes for our new business.
mistake.right: We have high hopes for our new business.
mistake.why: German *große Hoffnungen* tempts learners to say *big hopes*; the usual English adjective is *high*.

entries.related: *pin your hopes on* — depend on one thing to succeed; *expect great things from* — similar; *don't get your hopes up* — the opposite, a warning not to expect too much.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Describes something that should have happened or been done a long time ago.
entries.usage: Common in news, opinion pieces and conversation, often with approval: the thing is good, but it came late. Typical nouns are *change, repairs, apology, raise, recognition* and *visit*. It can follow a verb (*The change is long overdue*) or come before a noun, where it is usually hyphenated (*a long-overdue apology*).
entries.pattern: be long overdue; a long-overdue + noun
examples: I finally went to the dentist yesterday; that checkup was **long overdue**.
The town is finally making **long-overdue** repairs to the high school's leaky roof.
After ten years without a raise, a pay increase for the nurses is **long overdue**.

drill.sentence: We haven't seen each other since college, so this weekend trip is {{long overdue}}.
drill.hint: should have happened years ago (the adverb is not *way*)

entries.related: *overdue* — late, also for bills and library books; *better late than never* — said when something good finally happens; *premature* — the opposite, too early.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To stop noticing how much time is passing, usually because you are busy or enjoying yourself.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often as an apology or an excuse for being late: *Sorry, I lost track of time.* You can also *lose track of* money, people or a story. The opposite is *keep track of time*.
entries.pattern: lose track of time (+ -ing)
examples: Sorry I'm late; I was reading and completely **lost track of time**.
Kids **lose track of time** so easily when they're playing video games.
We were talking so much at dinner that we **lost track of time** and missed the last train.

drill.sentence: Working in the garden is so relaxing that I often {{lose track of time}} and forget to eat lunch.
drill.hint: stop noticing how late it is (the verb is not *forget*)

entries.related: *lose track of* + noun — stop knowing where something is or what is happening; *keep track of time* — the opposite; *time flies* — informal, time passes quickly.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To have the right to have or do something, often because of a law, a contract or a rule.
entries.usage: Common in law, employment, consumer rights and everyday arguments. Patterns are *be entitled to* + noun (*a refund, paid leave*) and *be entitled to* + verb. *You're entitled to your opinion* politely ends a disagreement, while *entitled* alone (*he's so entitled*) is negative and means someone expects special treatment.
entries.pattern: be entitled to + noun / to + verb
examples: If the airline cancels your flight, you're **entitled to** a full refund.
At my company, full-time employees **are entitled to** fifteen days of paid vacation a year.
You're **entitled to** your opinion, but I still think the movie was terrible.

drill.sentence: As a member of the gym, you're {{entitled to}} two free sessions with a personal trainer.
drill.hint: have a right to (the adjective is not *eligible*)

mistake.wrong: You are entitled for a refund.
mistake.right: You are entitled to a refund.
mistake.why: The preposition is *to*; *for* belongs to *eligible for*.

entries.related: *eligible for* — meeting the conditions to get something; *have a right to* — similar, a bit more general; *entitlement* — the noun, sometimes negative.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: A feeling of calm because you know that you do not need to worry about something.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and advertising, especially for insurance, alarm systems and warranties. Patterns are *give / bring someone peace of mind*, *for (your own) peace of mind* and *have peace of mind*. It is uncountable, so it takes no *a*.
entries.pattern: give someone peace of mind; for (your own) peace of mind
examples: Knowing that a neighbor checks on my mom every day gives me **peace of mind**.
We paid a little extra for travel insurance, just for **peace of mind**.
Some parents buy their kids phones mainly for their own **peace of mind**.

drill.sentence: Getting the car checked before a long road trip gives you real {{peace of mind}}.
drill.hint: a calm feeling that you don't need to worry (three words; not *reassurance*)

mistake.wrong: The extended warranty gives you a peace of mind.
mistake.right: The extended warranty gives you peace of mind.
mistake.why: *Peace of mind* is uncountable, so it takes no *a*.

entries.related: *reassurance* — something that removes a worry; *rest easy* — informal, stop worrying; *anxiety* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To happen exactly as was planned, without problems.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and work updates, very often in the negative: *Things didn't go according to plan.* There is no article before *plan*. *If all goes according to plan, …* introduces the result you expect.
entries.pattern: go according to plan; if all goes according to plan, …
examples: If everything **goes according to plan**, we'll move into the new house in June.
Our camping trip didn't exactly **go according to plan**: it rained for three days straight.
The rescue **went according to plan**, and all twelve miners were brought out safely.

drill.sentence: The surprise party {{went according to plan}} until my sister walked in an hour early.
drill.hint: happened just as intended (not *as planned* or *smoothly*)

entries.related: *go as planned* — same; *go smoothly* — happen without problems; *go wrong* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To earn the money you need to pay for food, housing and other basic costs.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and journalism. Patterns are *make a living as* + job, *make a living (by)* + *-ing* and *make a living from* + noun. The question *What do you do for a living?* is the standard way to ask about someone's job; *earn a living* is the same, a little more formal.
entries.pattern: make a living as + job / (by) + -ing / from + noun
examples: It's hard to **make a living** as a musician unless you also teach.
My grandfather **made a living** fixing shoes in the same small shop for forty years.
Many fishermen in the town can no longer **make a living** from the sea.

drill.sentence: She quit her office job and now {{makes a living}} selling handmade jewelry online.
drill.hint: gets the money she needs to live (the verb is not *earns*)

mistake.wrong: She earns her life as a translator.
mistake.right: She makes a living as a translator.
mistake.why: Learners translate French *gagner sa vie* or Spanish *ganarse la vida* word for word; English says *make a living* or *earn a living*.

entries.related: *earn a living* — same, slightly more formal; *make ends meet* — just manage to pay your bills; *scrape by* — survive with very little money.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A convincing reason for or against something, one that is hard to reject.
entries.usage: Common in debate, writing, law, business and serious conversation. Patterns are *a strong argument for / against* + noun or *-ing* and *make a strong argument that …*. Here *argument* means a reason, not a quarrel; for a fight, say *a big argument* or *a heated argument*.
entries.pattern: a strong argument for / against + noun / -ing; make a strong argument that …
examples: Lower rent is **a strong argument** for moving out of the city.
Her lawyer made **a strong argument** that the contract had never been valid.
The fact that she's never missed a deadline is **a strong argument** in her favor.

drill.sentence: The low crime rate and the good schools are {{a strong argument}} for raising kids in this town.
drill.hint: a convincing reason (the adjective is not *good* or *compelling*; the noun is not *case*)

mistake.wrong: My parents had a strong argument last night.
mistake.right: My parents had a big argument last night.
mistake.why: For a quarrel, natives say *a big* or *a heated argument*; *a strong argument* is a convincing reason.

entries.related: *a compelling argument* — more formal, very convincing; *a strong case for* — a set of good reasons; *a weak argument* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To understand words in their basic, exact sense, and so miss a joke, an exaggeration or an idiom.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often as a warning or a joke: *Don't take it literally.* The object goes between *take* and *literally*: *take it / that / someone literally*. Don't confuse it with *take something seriously*, which is about importance, not meaning.
entries.pattern: take something / someone literally
examples: When I told my four-year-old to "hop in the car," he **took it literally** and hopped across the driveway.
She said the party was "totally dead," but I don't think we should **take that literally**.
Sarcasm is hard to read in emails, so some coworkers may **take your jokes literally**.

drill.sentence: When Grandpa says he walked ten miles to school every day, don't {{take him literally}}; it was about two.
drill.hint: believe his exact words (the adverb is not *seriously*)

entries.related: *take something at face value* — accept it as it first appears; *read between the lines* — find the hidden meaning; *take something seriously* — treat it as important.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Accidentally, without meaning to, usually because you did the wrong thing or chose the wrong person or object.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, usually after the verb phrase: *I deleted the file by mistake.* *By accident* is very similar, but *by mistake* stresses an error, while *by accident* stresses chance. In official messages, *in error* is the formal version.
entries.pattern: do something by mistake
examples: Sorry, I think I took your umbrella **by mistake**; they look exactly the same.
The bank charged us twice **by mistake**, but they refunded the money the next day.
I hit "Reply All" **by mistake** and sent my complaint to the whole team.

drill.sentence: Someone at the post office delivered our neighbor's package to our house {{by mistake}}.
drill.hint: through an error, not on purpose (not *by accident* or *in error*)

entries.related: *by accident* — by chance, without planning; *in error* — formal, used in official messages; *on purpose* — the opposite, deliberately.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To agree on a solution after each side accepts less than it originally wanted.
entries.usage: Common in news about negotiations, at work and in family life. Patterns are *reach a compromise on / over* + issue and *reach a compromise with* someone; *come to a compromise* and *work out a compromise* are also natural. Adjectives like *fair*, *reasonable* or *last-minute* often go before *compromise*.
entries.pattern: reach a compromise (with + someone) on / over + issue
examples: I wanted a beach vacation and my wife wanted the mountains, so we **reached a compromise**: a lake in Maine.
After weeks of arguing about the thermostat, my roommate and I finally **reached a compromise**.
After a long fight, the kids **reached a compromise** on who gets the front seat.

drill.sentence: Neither side wanted to give up anything at first, but by midnight the two companies had {{reached a compromise}}.
drill.hint: agreed, with each giving something up (the verb is not *come to* or *work out*; the noun is not *agreement*)

mistake.wrong: After a long discussion, we closed a compromise.
mistake.right: After a long discussion, we reached a compromise.
mistake.why: German *einen Kompromiss schließen* is *reach* or *come to a compromise* in English; *close* doesn't work with *compromise*.

entries.related: *meet someone halfway* — informal, each give up something; *strike a deal* — agree, often in business; *reach a deadlock* — the opposite, no agreement is possible.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An approximate calculation of a number, a cost or an amount of time that is not meant to be exact.
entries.usage: Common at work, in planning and home repairs, and in everyday questions like *Can you give me a rough estimate?* Patterns are *give / make a rough estimate (of* + noun*)*; informally, people also say *a ballpark figure*. *Rough* here means approximate, not violent or unpleasant.
entries.pattern: give (someone) / make a rough estimate (of + noun)
examples: The plumber gave us **a rough estimate** of eight hundred dollars, but said it could change.
Can you give me **a rough estimate** of how long the drive will take?
**A rough estimate** puts the crowd at the free concert at about two thousand people.

drill.sentence: Before the roofers start, ask for {{a rough estimate}} so the final bill isn't a shock.
drill.hint: an approximate figure (not *a ballpark figure*; the noun is not *quote*, *idea* or *guess*)

entries.related: *a ballpark figure* — informal, from baseball, an approximate number; *a quote* — a fixed price offered by a worker or company; *an exact figure* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To decide that something is true after thinking about it carefully, often over some time.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, a bit more formal than *decide* or *realize*. It is followed by a *that* clause, with no comma before *that*; *reach the conclusion that* is a more formal variant. *Come to a conclusion* without a clause means to make a decision: *We haven't come to a conclusion yet.*
entries.pattern: come to the conclusion that + clause
examples: After three months of arguing, we **came to the conclusion that** we just weren't right for each other.
I've **come to the conclusion that** paying for a gym I never use is a waste of money.
Investigators **came to the conclusion that** the crash was caused by ice on the road.

drill.sentence: After reading every review online, my sister {{came to the conclusion that}} the cheaper laptop was just as good.
drill.hint: decided, after careful thought (a longer phrase than *concluded*)

mistake.wrong: I came to the conclusion, that we need a bigger apartment.
mistake.right: I came to the conclusion that we need a bigger apartment.
mistake.why: English puts no comma before a *that* clause, unlike German before *dass*.

entries.related: *conclude that* — one word, more formal; *reach the conclusion that* — more formal; *jump to conclusions* — decide too quickly, without enough facts.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A very small possibility that something will happen.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports and news. Patterns are *a slim chance of* + noun or *-ing* and *There's a slim chance (that) …*, often with *only* before it. *Slim* also goes with *odds* and *hopes*, and *slim to none* is a fixed informal phrase: *His chances are slim to none.*
entries.pattern: (only) a slim chance of + -ing / that …
examples: There's only **a slim chance** of rain tomorrow, so the picnic is still on.
The team still has **a slim chance** of making the playoffs if they win their last three games.
Doctors said he had **a slim chance** of walking again, but he proved them wrong.

drill.sentence: I know there's only {{a slim chance}} that the airline will find my lost bag, but I'm still hoping.
drill.hint: a tiny possibility (the adjective is not *small*, *slight* or *remote*)

entries.related: *Fat chance!* — sarcastic, meaning no chance at all; *a long shot* — an attempt unlikely to succeed; *a good chance* — the opposite, quite likely.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To start to manage, direct or have power over something, often in a difficult situation.
entries.usage: Common at work, in sports, health and self-help writing, and in news about companies or emergencies. The pattern is *take (full) control of* + noun, with no article before *control*. *Be in control of* describes the state; *take control* describes the moment of change.
entries.pattern: take (full) control of + noun
examples: After her divorce, she decided to **take control of** her finances and made a strict budget.
The co-pilot **took control of** the plane when the captain suddenly felt sick.
Our team **took control of** the game in the second half and never looked back.

drill.sentence: When the kitchen fire started, my aunt calmly {{took control of}} the situation and got everyone outside.
drill.hint: started managing (the noun is not *charge*; the verb is not *got*)

mistake.wrong: She took the control of the meeting.
mistake.right: She took control of the meeting.
mistake.why: In this phrase *control* takes no article: *take control of*.

entries.related: *take charge (of)* — very similar, stresses leadership; *take over* — take control from someone else; *lose control (of)* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To happen or work without problems or delays.
entries.usage: Common at work, in events, travel and family life, about plans, machines, systems and organizations. Typical frames are *run smoothly*, *keep things running smoothly* and *make sure everything runs smoothly*. For a single event that is over, *go smoothly* is also very common: *The move went smoothly.*
entries.pattern: run smoothly; keep things running smoothly
examples: Thanks to hundreds of volunteers, the marathon **ran smoothly** despite the heat.
My car is **running smoothly** again now that the mechanic has replaced the spark plugs.
A good office manager keeps everything **running smoothly** behind the scenes.

drill.sentence: With three kids and two jobs, we need a strict schedule to keep the house {{running smoothly}}.
drill.hint: working without problems (the verb is not *going*; the adverb is not *well*)

entries.related: *go smoothly* — happen without problems, usually one event; *like clockwork* — informal, perfectly and on time; *hit a snag* — the opposite, meet an unexpected problem.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A large amount of work that a person or a team has to do.
entries.usage: Common at work, at school and in health care, often as a complaint or an explanation. Patterns are *have / handle / manage a heavy workload*, and job ads often ask for someone who *can handle a heavy workload*. *Workload* is one word, and *heavy* is its most common adjective.
entries.pattern: have / handle / manage a heavy workload
examples: Nurses on the night shift often have **a heavy workload** and very few breaks.
With five classes this semester, my daughter is struggling with **a heavy workload**.
Because of **a heavy workload**, the clinic can't take new patients until March.

drill.sentence: Sorry I haven't called in a while; I've had {{a heavy workload}} since my coworker quit.
drill.hint: a lot to do at the office (the adjective is not *big*; not *a full plate*)

entries.related: *have a lot on your plate* — informal, have many tasks; *be swamped* — informal, extremely busy; *a light workload* — the opposite.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Earlier than the time that was planned.
entries.usage: Common in work updates, construction, travel and news about projects. Patterns are *be / finish / arrive ahead of schedule* and *two weeks ahead of schedule*. *On schedule* means at the planned time and *behind schedule* means late; Americans say *schedule* as /ˈskɛdʒul/ (SKEJ-ool).
entries.pattern: (two weeks) ahead of schedule
examples: The new bridge opened three months **ahead of schedule**, which almost never happens.
The movers showed up an hour **ahead of schedule**, so we were still packing.
We finished the hike an hour **ahead of schedule** and had time for a swim.

drill.sentence: Thanks to the dry weather, the farmers finished the harvest a week {{ahead of schedule}}.
drill.hint: earlier than planned (the noun is not *time*)

entries.related: *on schedule* — at the planned time; *ahead of time* — in advance, earlier than needed; *behind schedule* — the opposite, late.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To try another way of dealing with a problem or task, usually because the first way did not work.
entries.usage: Common at work, in teaching, parenting, sports and everyday problem solving. Patterns are *take a different approach (to* + noun or *-ing)* and *try a different approach*; *a completely different approach* adds emphasis. The usual preposition after *approach* is *to*: *a new approach to learning*.
entries.pattern: take a different approach (to + noun / -ing)
examples: Yelling at the kids wasn't working, so we decided to **take a different approach** and reward good behavior instead.
This season the coach is **taking a different approach** to practice, with fewer drills and more games.
Instead of sending another long email, I **took a different approach** and just called her.

drill.sentence: The diet wasn't working, so my doctor suggested I {{take a different approach}} and focus on smaller portions instead.
drill.hint: deal with it in another way (the verb is not *try*; the adjective is not *new*)

entries.related: *try a new tack* — change your method; *rethink* — think again about a plan; *stay the course* — the opposite, continue in the same way.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A limited amount of money that must be spent very carefully.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, business, travel and home life. The usual patterns are *on a tight budget* (*We're traveling on a tight budget*) and *work with / stick to a tight budget*. *Tight* also describes money in general: *Money is tight this month.*
entries.pattern: on a tight budget; work with / stick to a tight budget
examples: We're on **a tight budget** this month, so we're cooking at home instead of eating out.
The film was shot in six weeks on **a tight budget**, with a cast of unknown actors.
**A tight budget** forced the school to cancel its spring field trip.

drill.sentence: As students, we traveled around Europe on {{a tight budget}}, sleeping in hostels and eating a lot of bread.
drill.hint: very little money to spend (the adjective is not *small*, *limited* or *low*; not *a shoestring*)

entries.related: *on a shoestring* — informal, with very little money; *cash-strapped* — short of money; *money is no object* — the opposite.

entries.term: take the opportunity to do something
entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To use a chance or an occasion to do something, often something you have wanted to do.
entries.usage: Very common in speeches, emails and meetings, often in polite formulas: *I'd like to take this opportunity to thank everyone …* Patterns are *take the opportunity to* + verb and *take this opportunity to* + verb, the second mostly in formal speech and writing. In casual speech, *use the chance to* is more relaxed.
entries.pattern: take the / this opportunity to + verb
examples: I'd like to **take this opportunity to** thank everyone who helped organize tonight's fundraiser.
While I was in Boston for work, I **took the opportunity to** visit my old college roommate.
Stuck at home with a broken ankle, I **took the opportunity to** finally learn to knit.

drill.sentence: With the whole family together for the reunion, we {{took the opportunity to}} record my great-uncle's stories about growing up on a farm.
drill.hint: didn't waste the moment (the verb is not *seized* or *used*; the noun is not *chance*)

entries.related: *seize the opportunity* — stronger, act quickly and eagerly; *jump at the chance* — informal, accept eagerly; *miss the opportunity* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A person who smokes a lot of cigarettes, usually every day.
entries.usage: Common in medicine, news and conversation, and fairly neutral in tone. *Heavy* is the usual adjective for amounts of smoking and drinking: *a heavy drinker*, *heavy drinking*. The opposite is *a light smoker*, and *a chain smoker* lights one cigarette right after another.
entries.pattern: a heavy smoker / drinker
examples: Her father was **a heavy smoker** for forty years and only quit after a heart attack.
Life insurance costs a lot more if you're **a heavy smoker**.
As **a heavy smoker**, he gets out of breath after one flight of stairs.

drill.sentence: Even though she was {{a heavy smoker}} for years, her lungs recovered surprisingly well after she quit.
drill.hint: someone who smoked a lot every day (the describing word is not *big* or *chain*)

mistake.wrong: My father was a strong smoker.
mistake.right: My father was a heavy smoker.
mistake.why: German *starker Raucher* is *heavy smoker* in English; *strong* isn't used for amounts of smoking or drinking.

entries.related: *a chain smoker* — lights one cigarette after another; *a light smoker* — the opposite; *a social smoker* — smokes only at parties or with friends.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To judge ideas, claims and information carefully, looking for evidence and weak points, instead of simply accepting them.
entries.usage: Common in education, job ads, journalism and discussions about media and news. Typical frames are *teach students to think critically*, *the ability to think critically* and *think critically about* + noun. The noun phrase *critical thinking* is just as common; neither means being negative or complaining.
entries.pattern: think critically (about + noun)
examples: Good teachers don't just give answers; they teach kids to **think critically**.
Before you share that article, **think critically** about who wrote it and why.
A good journalist **thinks critically** about every source, even a friendly one.

drill.sentence: With so many fake videos online, it's more important than ever to {{think critically}} about what you watch.
drill.hint: question and judge ideas, not just accept them (the adverb is not *carefully* or *clearly*)

entries.related: *critical thinking* — the noun phrase; *be skeptical of* — doubt claims until there is proof; *accept something blindly* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To accept, or be made to accept, responsibility for something bad, whether or not it was really your fault.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news, work and sports. The pattern is *take the blame for* + noun or *-ing*; *get the blame* stresses that other people put it on you. Compare *be to blame*, which says who is really responsible.
entries.pattern: take the blame for + noun / -ing
examples: The waiter **took the blame** for the wrong order, even though the kitchen had mixed it up.
The coach **took the blame for** the loss and said his players had done everything right.
Why should I **take the blame for** a mistake my manager made?

drill.sentence: When the dog ate the birthday cake, my sister let me {{take the blame}}, even though she'd left it on the table.
drill.hint: be the one held responsible (the verb is not *get*)

mistake.wrong: He took the guilt for the accident.
mistake.right: He took the blame for the accident.
mistake.why: German *Schuld* can mean *blame* or *guilt*; for responsibility, English says *take the blame*, while *guilt* is a feeling.

entries.related: *take the fall* — informal, accept punishment for others; *shoulder the blame* — slightly more formal; *pass the buck* — the opposite, push responsibility onto someone else.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Happening now and not yet finished.
entries.usage: Common on signs, in work updates, news and formal notices: *Meeting in progress*, *Construction in progress*. It follows a noun or the verb *be*: *The investigation is still in progress.* *A work in progress* is a fixed phrase for something, or someone, still being developed.
entries.pattern: be (still) in progress; noun + in progress
examples: Please keep your voice down; there's a test **in progress** in room twelve.
Repairs on the elevator are still **in progress**, so please use the stairs.
The game was already **in progress** when we finally found our seats.

drill.sentence: The sign on the door said "Meeting {{in progress}}," so I waited in the hall until they finished.
drill.hint: currently happening, not finished (not *underway* or *in session*)

entries.related: *underway* — already started, often of large projects; *a work in progress* — something still being developed; *completed* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A very noticeable way of pronouncing a language that shows where someone comes from.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, and neutral as a description, though commenting on someone's accent to their face can sound rude. Patterns are *have a strong (Southern / Boston / German) accent* and *speak with a strong accent*; *a thick* or *heavy accent* means the same. The opposite is *a slight* or *faint accent*.
entries.pattern: have / speak with a strong (+ origin) accent
examples: My uncle has **a strong Boston accent**, so "car" sounds like "cah" when he says it.
Even after thirty years in Texas, my mother still speaks with **a strong Italian accent**.
The tour guide had such **a strong accent** that half the group couldn't follow her.

drill.sentence: He grew up in Glasgow and still has {{a strong accent}}, so Americans sometimes ask him to repeat things.
drill.hint: a very noticeable regional way of speaking (the adjective is not *thick*, *heavy* or *Scottish*)

entries.related: *a thick* / *heavy accent* — same, sometimes less kind; *a slight accent* — the opposite, barely noticeable; *a dialect* — a regional form with its own words and grammar, not just pronunciation.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To feel satisfied with something you do or own, and so do it with care because it matters to you.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, job ads and descriptions of work and character. The pattern is *take (great) pride in* + noun or *-ing*, with no article before *pride*. *Be proud of* is the plain equivalent, while *take pride in* stresses ongoing care and effort.
entries.pattern: take (great) pride in + noun / -ing
examples: My dad **takes pride in** his lawn and mows it every Saturday morning.
The restaurant **takes great pride in** using only local ingredients.
She **took pride in** never missing a single day of school.

drill.sentence: The old carpenter {{takes pride in}} every chair he builds, and it shows in the details.
drill.hint: feels satisfied with and cares about (not *is proud of*)

mistake.wrong: We take pride of our customer service.
mistake.right: We take pride in our customer service.
mistake.why: *Proud* takes *of*, but *take pride* takes *in*.

entries.related: *be proud of* — plainer; *pride yourself on* — be proud of a quality or skill you have; *do a sloppy job* — the opposite, work without care.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: A feeling of satisfaction after you have achieved something difficult.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, interviews, education and self-help writing. Patterns are *give someone a sense of accomplishment*, *feel a (real / great) sense of accomplishment* and *a sense of accomplishment from* + *-ing*. *A sense of achievement* means the same and is more common in British English.
entries.pattern: give someone / feel a (real) sense of accomplishment
examples: Finishing my first marathon gave me **a sense of accomplishment** I'll never forget.
Kids get **a real sense of accomplishment** from building something with their own hands.
Some days I answer emails for eight hours and go home without any **sense of accomplishment**.

drill.sentence: After changing my first flat tire by myself, I felt {{a sense of accomplishment}} for the rest of the day.
drill.hint: a feeling of satisfaction at doing something hard (the last noun is not *achievement* or *pride*)

entries.related: *a sense of achievement* — same, more common in British English; *a sense of pride* — feeling proud; *a sense of failure* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To start to want to learn about something, or to become involved with something or someone.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, parenting, school reports and work. The pattern is *take an interest in* + noun or *-ing*, often with *keen*, *real* or *active* before *interest*. *Be interested in* describes a state, while *take an interest* suggests a new or active involvement, often in someone else's life.
entries.pattern: take a (keen / real) interest in + noun / -ing
examples: My son has suddenly **taken an interest in** cooking, so dinner has gotten a lot more creative.
A good mentor **takes a real interest in** your career, not just in what you can do for them.
When my dad retired, he **took an interest in** local history and started volunteering at the historical society.

drill.sentence: Ever since her trip to Japan, Emma has {{taken an interest in}} learning the language.
drill.hint: begun to want to know more about (the verb is not *developed*; not *gotten into*)

mistake.wrong: She has taken an interest for gardening.
mistake.right: She has taken an interest in gardening.
mistake.why: *Interest* takes *in*; German *Interesse für* tempts learners to use *for*.

entries.related: *be interested in* — describes the state; *develop an interest in* — similar, more gradual; *lose interest in* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To express ideas and information clearly, so that other people understand them as you intended.
entries.usage: Typical of job ads, résumés, performance reviews, education and advice about relationships. Patterns are *communicate effectively with* someone and *the ability to communicate effectively*. In casual speech it can sound like business jargon, so people often say *get your point across* instead.
entries.pattern: communicate effectively (with + someone)
examples: Doctors need to **communicate effectively** with patients who are scared or confused.
Babies can't talk yet, but they **communicate** surprisingly **effectively** by crying.
The job posting says applicants must be able to **communicate effectively** in English and Spanish.

drill.sentence: Our family therapist taught us to {{communicate effectively}} instead of yelling at each other.
drill.hint: express ourselves in a way the others understand (the adverb is not *better*, *well* or *clearly*)

entries.related: *get your point across* — informal, make people understand your idea; *make yourself understood* — manage to be understood, often in a foreign language; *miscommunicate* — the opposite.
